headlines.title: San Jose officer hospitalized after shootout leaves robbery suspect dead
headlines.description: A San Jose police sergeant who was shot by an armed robbery suspect suffered critical injuries but has since been stabilized, police said Wednesday. The confrontation unfolded Tuesday after officers spotted a suspect wanted in connection with two armed robberies reported over the weekend, according to the San Jose Police Department. When officers approached the suspect, police said he pulled out a firearm and drove away, hitting at least one other vehicle along the way. The suspect abandoned the vehicle near Lick Avenue and Goodyear Street and continued fleeing on foot, police said. He eventually reached the area of Almaden Avenue and Floyd Street, where police said he ran to a nearby home occupied by a young family and forced his way inside to hide. Two officers followed the suspect into the home, where the suspect opened fire and struck a police sergeant, according to SJPD. The suspect was also shot and died at the scene. Brett Bynaster, whose children and grandchildren were inside the home, said they hid in a closet before officers arrived and got them out safely. “Officers busted the door down,” Bynaster said, praising their bravery. “They rushed everyone out and we’re incredibly grateful.” Police said the suspect was wanted in connection with two armed robberies over the weekend in which he allegedly threatened two people with a weapon described as a long gun. Detectives are continuing to investigate the shooting, and police said additional details are expected to be released Wednesday afternoon. The shooting was San Jose police’s second officer-involved shooting of 2026.

headlines.title: San Jose police arrest alleged strong-armed jewelry thieves
headlines.description: Police in San Jose arrested an alleged ring of jewelry thieves who forcibly robbed elderly people, the department said Tuesday. Last Thursday just before 3 p.m., officers in San Jose responded to a strong-armed robbery in a parking lot in the 5300 block of Almaden Expressway. According to the victim, who is an elderly woman, a woman approached her and forcibly took her ring and gold chain necklace before taking off in a car being driven by a man. Investigators were able to identify the car used in the robbery and on Friday, the car was located in Concord, where someone else reported a strong-armed robbery outside of a business. The suspects’ vehicle was then tracked through license plate cameras back to San Jose at a business located in the 2200 block of Senter Road. Officers made contact with the suspects and two men and one woman were detained: Ruxandra Constantin, 30, Caldararu Constantin, 36, and Constantin Constantin, 34. While the trio was being arrested, another elderly woman approached police and said she had just been robbed of her gold chain necklace, allegedly by the suspects. Police said they located a bag with gold and jewelry in it in the possession of Ruxandra Constantin. Investigators believe the three are responsible for an additional grand theft of a gold chain necklace on Aug. 16 in a parking lot in the 5300 block of Almaden Expressway, where an elderly man was robbed. According to police, chain snatch robberies have been an increasing trend not only in the city of San Jose but throughout the Bay Area. “In these cases, the suspects typically approach elderly victims walking in public and forcibly remove the gold chain necklace off the person,” the San Jose Police Department said. “Often times, the suspects will use distraction techniques, such as selling jewelry, striking up a conversation, or swapping the jewelry out without the victim’s knowledge.” Due to the nature of these crimes, detectives believe there may be additional victims. Anyone with information about these cases or similar cases is asked to contact Detective Thandi at 4415@sanjoseca.gov or 408-277-4166.

headlines.title: Napa Valley wineries serve up new ‘experiences' amid sobering economic downturn
headlines.description: Tourism to Napa Valley historically brings in more than $2 billion each year, but fewer visitors and higher costs have winemakers across the region worried about an increasingly difficult financial landscape. “It’s not just the big guys that are getting hurt, it’s not just the little guys that getting hurt, it’s everybody in between,” said Christi Ficeli, owner of Goosecross Cellars in Napa Valley. “This economy is hard for everybody, even the people that own wineries in Napa.” This economy is hard for everybody, even the people that own wineries in Napa Christi Ficeli, owner of Goosecross Cellars in Napa Valley Ficeli, who runs the family-owned winery with her husband, Dave Ficeli, says visitation at the winery is down 40% from five years ago. “Cash is tight right now – the economy is tough on us,” she said. “Prices are increasing.” While Napa’s famed vintages are made locally, supplies often come from abroad and tariffs have resulted in higher prices. Wine barrels from France, glass bottles from China, and corks from Portugal have all increased in price, according to Ficeli, and rising gas prices have made those supplies even more expensive to transport. “Our costs have gone up 10% to 12% and our pricing has gone up 1% to 2%,” Ficeli said. “We’re absorbing a lot of that here.” Christi Ficeli has run Goosecross Cellars in Napa Valley for the past 13 years with her husband Dave Ficeli. To offset higher costs, Ficeli’s winery is now focusing on more than just wine. To attract new customers and keep guests coming back, Goosecross has been hosting an array of events at its vineyard, including movie nights and comedy shows. “We’ve started doing more events because I think people want experience – they want things that are different,” she said. “We’re trying to bring some new and exciting things to the visitors that are here in Napa.” Ficeli is also investing in customer retention by recently expanding her staff from 12 to 13 employees, with the newest hire dedicated to keeping existing customers. Ellie Leigh was recently hired for the newly created customer-retention position. “Personal touch points, handwritten invitations, and notes has been really top of mind,” Leigh told Ficeli during a recent meeting at the winery. Ellie Leigh is the newest hire at Goosecross Cellars, where she is responsible for retaining customers and boosting wine subscriptions as the winery’s head of estate partnerships. I know it’s going to hurt to add another staff member, but if she can save a customer from leaving our program and keep them around for a little bit longer, it’s going to be worth every penny I’m spending on her. Winery owner Christi Ficeli explains why she hired a new employee to focus on customer retention “I know it’s going to hurt to add another staff member, but if she can save a customer from leaving our program and keep them around for a little bit longer, it’s going to be worth every penny I’m spending on her,” Ficeli told the Investigative Unit. “It’s so much more expensive to gain a new customer than to keep one.” For winery owners across Napa Valley, simply resting on the region’s laurels as a top-tier destination may no longer be enough to keep customers coming through the door. “It definitely has changed,” Ficeli said. “Mostly because there’s less people coming to Napa.” The region welcomed 3.8 million visitors last year, about 50,000 fewer than visited in 2018, according to Visit Napa Valley, Napa County’s tourism marketing organization. While Napa visitation has rebounded in recent years, it remains below its pre-pandemic peak. At the same time, fewer Americans are drinking wine. Only about 29% of adults in America drink wine compared to 34% three years ago, according to the Wine Market Council, a research firm that tracks consumer wine spending. Napa Valley tourism rates near pre-pandemic levels Adding to the challenge is the cost of traveling to wine country. The average hotel room in Napa Valley now costs about $420 a night – a 25% increase since before the pandemic, according to Visit Napa Valley. “We’ve done some estimates, it’s probably about $5,000 just to stay here for the weekend before you even walk through the door of a winery,” Ficeli said. “Hotel, flight, rental car, and food … all up.” Tasting prices have also climbed. The average tasting fee in Napa is now about $80, according to a recent wine industry report by Silicon Valley Bank. Food & Drink Jun 10 Napa County Apr 22, 2025 “We’re going through a really tough time,” said Tom Davies, who runs V. Sattui, a 50-year-old winery with more than 100 employees. “What’s at stake here is the sustainability of our wine industry.” Davies said the economy forced him to change pricing, too, but not in the way you might think. Two days a week, he dropped his tasting fee to zero to attract new business. We have to open our doors wider. Tom Davies, President and Managing Partner of V. Sattui Winery Tom Davies is president and managing partner of V. Sattui Winery in Napa Valley. “We have to open our doors wider,” Davies said. “I want to even be more accessible than we’ve ever been before.” Davies said the move to offer three complimentary pours has boosted wine sales. So much so, he’s now offering the free tasting menu three days a week. “We’re selling more wine than we were when we were charging every day,” he said. Davies remembers when all tastings in Napa were free. He said his idea to bring free tastings back is a nod to the past and an investment in the future – not only for his winery but for the entire Napa Valley. “The real payoff would be down the road when we can get the kind of visitation back to the vineyards that we had back 10 years ago,” he said. “I just want to make sure we can continue on.” Whether it’s larger wineries like his or smaller ones like Christi Ficeli’s down the road, the financial strain has been hard to swallow. I would say 2026 is one of the hardest years we’ve had so far outside of Covid. Christi Ficeli has run Goosecross Cellars for the past 13 years with her husband Winery owner Christi Ficeli takes Senior Investigative Reporter Bigad Shaban on a tour of her Napa Valley vineyard at Goosecross Cellars. “I would say 2026 is one of the hardest years we’ve had so far outside of Covid,” she said. “We’re working to cut costs everywhere we can.” Despite the financial squeeze, Ficeli remains hopeful. Like so many winery owners in Napa Valley, she’s holding on to a glass-half-full kind of optimism. “I love what I do,” she said. “When people come to Napa, they’re celebrating – 99.9% of the people who walk through our door are already happy and I get to make them that much happier by giving them an experience.” Contact The Investigative Unit submit tips | 1-888-996-TIPS | e-mail Bigad Follow @BigadShaban on social media Bigad Shaban This story uses functionality that may not work in our app. Click here to open the story in your web browser.

headlines.title: VTA Orange Line fully reopens after electrical issue
headlines.description: VTA’s Orange Line returned to full service Wednesday morning after an electrical issue disrupted service at four stations for about a day, transit officials said. VTA crews worked overnight to make repairs after an electrical line issue cut power to four Orange Line stations at about 6 a.m. Tuesday. Full service resumed at all Orange Line stations at 7 a.m. Wednesday, according to VTA. The agency did not immediately provide additional details about what caused the electrical issue.

headlines.title: Contractor accused of misconduct in cleanup at Hunters Point shipyard agrees to pay $57M
headlines.description: Tetra Tech EC Inc., a company that oversaw cleanup of radiological material at the site of the former Hunters Point Naval Shipyard in San Francisco, has agreed to settle a lawsuit that accused the company of manipulating contaminated soil samples, the U.S. Department of Justice announced this week. “By falsifying work claims and manipulating critical data, Tetra Tech put its own financial interests ahead of its commitments to the Department of the Navy, potentially placing the health and safety of the American people at risk,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Brian Merkal of the Naval Criminal Investigative Service’s Economic Crimes Field Office in a statement. The $57 million settlement marks the culmination of a controversy surrounding Tetra Tech EC’s work at Hunters Point Naval Shipyard. The company contracted with the U.S. Navy between 2003 and 2014 to remediate radiation contamination at the shipyard. The shipyard was occupied by the Navy from 1945 to 1974, during which the Naval Radiological Defense Laboratory conducted research on the effects of radiation and atomic weapons. The site was also used to decommission radioactive ships, leading to the accumulation of radionuclides contaminating the surrounding soil and water. It was designated in 1989 as a federal Superfund site, which are areas contaminated with hazardous materials that require long-term cleanup. In 2012, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency accused Tetra Tech EC of falsifying radiological data of soil tests and misrepresenting soil samples after several whistleblowers from Tetra Tech EC spoke out. The EPA’s lawsuit alleged that the company instructed workers to throw out contaminated soil samples and replace them with “clean” samples for testing, according to the Department of Justice. It also accused the contractor of intentionally manipulating scan results of soil samples, actions that benefited Tetra Tech EC by receiving unearned contract award fees and avoiding the need to conduct additional remediation work. “This has been a critical project for the Hunters Point community and the federal government,” said U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian for the DOJ’s Northern District of California. “It should have been just as important to the contractor that the government selected and paid to perform radiological testing and remediation at the site.” Federal prosecutors highlighted that Tetra Tech EC agreeing to the settlement is not an admission of guilt. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Greenaction for Health and Environmental Justice, an organization that has previously sued the Navy over its cleanup process at the site, and community groups from the Bayview Hunters Point neighborhood have been calling for a proper cleanup for decades. Greenaction’s executive director Bradley Angel welcomed the settlement as an important step in fighting for accountability. “It’s wonderful news,” Angel said in an interview. “It also vindicates what Greenaction and community groups have said for years and years, which is that the cleanup was inadequate. It was flawed. It was reckless. It was tainted.” But Angel said that the battle is far from over. With cleanup efforts still ongoing, Greenaction and community groups are demanding independent oversight of the Navy’s cleanup to help ensure thorough remediation. Earlier this year, the Navy discovered “unauthorized” radiological material stored in a cabinet of a secured building at the site. The Navy said the material was placed in the building by a former subcontractor at the site, potentially without obtaining proper licensing. “We still don’t trust the agencies because their track record has not earned the trust of the public,” Angel said. Greenaction and other local activists are also pushing for reparations for the residents of Bayview Hunters Point who have suffered adverse health effects that they say are associated with living near the former shipyard. The pollution emitted from the neighborhood’s history of industrial activities has been a contributing factor to poorer health outcomes for its residents, who have increased rates of asthma, respiratory diseases, and cancers compared to the rest of the city, according to the San Francisco Environment Department. “The concern is that there still needs to be justice for the residents of Bayview Hunters Point, who continue to suffer harm and severe and profound health impacts from being exposed to radiation and toxic waste that was never properly cleaned up,” Angel said. “Tetra Tech was a big part of the problem, but not the whole problem.”

headlines.title: Alysa Liu taking a break from figure skating while looking ahead to next season
headlines.description: Olympic gold medalist Alysa Liu is taking a break from figure skating. The 2026 Milan Cortina star announced on social media that she will take the rest of the 2026-27 figure skating season off before returning for the 2027-28 season. “While people are announcing programs, imma take this time to announce that I will not be competing this season,” Liu wrote in an Instagram post. “I always want to challenge myself in new ways, so my artistry & skating can evolve. It’s important to me that my sport reflects my personal growth. I’m gonna take the time to recalibrate, fine-tune things & whatnot. So fear not, I’ll be back, & in the meantime I’ll be rooting for my teammates near & far. See yall soon!!” It’s been a whirlwind year for the Bay Area native, who was raised in Oakland. In February, Liu became the first American woman to win Olympic singles gold since Sarah Hughes in 2002. That breakout performance led to incredible opportunities off the ice, including sharing a moment with Taylor Swift, appearing in a music video for Laufey and attending the Louis Vuitton show at Paris Fashion Week. This isn’t the first time that Liu is stepping away from figure skating, but she didn’t have any plans to return the last time she did it. Following her 2022 Olympic debut, Liu retired at age 16 before returning unexpectedly two years later with a newfound love for the sport. Liu, now 21, dominated upon returning from her brief retirement. She won gold at the women’s world championships in 2025 before her Olympic run earlier this year. It’s unclear exactly where Liu will return to competition, but the earliest would be in July 2027. She had previously been scheduled to compete at Saatva Skate America from Nov. 13-15 in Everett, Washington. 2026 Milan Cortina Olympics Mar 2 2026 Milan Cortina Olympics Feb 25 2026 Milan Cortina Olympics Mar 4 Oakland's Olympic champ Alysa Liu surprises Jimmy Fallon, gifts him iconic wig

headlines.title: San Jose transportation worker killed while repairing streetlight
headlines.description: A San Jose Department of Transportation employee died Tuesday after being injured while repairing a streetlight, according to city officials. San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan, City Manager Jennifer Maguire, and Department of Transportation Director John Ristow issued a joint statement announcing the employee’s death while performing public service duties aimed at keeping drivers and pedestrians safe. City leaders did not immediately release the identity of the worker. “We are sad to share that a member of our City of San Jose family lost his life today while serving the public,” officials said in the statement. “We are deeply heartbroken about his passing and grateful for his public service.” Police said a box truck driver crashed into a crane truck at about 10:30 a.m. Tuesday in the area of Hillsdale and Narvaez avenues, causing a person inside the crane bucket to fall out. The victim was taken to a local hospital with life-threatening injuries, but he did not survive, police said. The driver of the box truck stayed at the scene and cooperated with investigators, police said. Following the incident, officials called on drivers to exercise caution near roadway work zones, urging the public to stay attentive, slow down, and provide adequate space for maintenance workers, construction crews, and emergency responders stopped in the street. “Our heartfelt condolences go out to his family, friends, and his department teammates during this incredibly difficult time,” the joint statement said. An investigation is ongoing.

headlines.title: Karol G surprises patients at Children's Hospital Oakland
headlines.description: Karol G rocked two sold-out shows at Levi’s Stadium last weekend, but her swing through the Bay Area didn’t stop there. The Latin pop star made a surprise visit to UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland, saying hello and bringing gifts to children being treated there, including Isabella Betancourt. “She just made me feel so happy and made me feel so special,” Betancourt said. Betancourt is being treated for epilepsy and said she hasn’t had a seizure in more than a year.

headlines.title: Instagram head defends platform safety efforts in federal trial over youth addiction claims
headlines.description: State attorneys challenged the head of Instagram over whether the platform does enough to protect young users during a landmark federal trial accusing parent company Meta of designing intentionally addictive and dangerous features. Adam Mosseri testified in Oakland federal court Tuesday as part of a lawsuit brought by 29 states against Meta. Mosseri, who has led Instagram since 2018, denied claims that he knowingly concealed negative data from the public regarding the platform’s impact on young users. Mosseri is the first high-profile Meta executive to take the stand, telling the jury that he and his team prioritize the safety of younger users. His testimony followed statements from former Instagram employees who alleged the company ignored internal data showing youth encountered higher rates of bullying, hate speech, violent content, and suicide-related material than adults. “I think it’s really a bellwether, as many are describing it, to see how we move forward and how platforms can be held accountable and will be held accountable by legal courts and the court of public opinion,” said Nora Benavidez, senior counsel at Free Press. Former employees also testified that Meta knew fewer users would utilize Instagram’s “Take a Break” feature unless it was set as a default. Mosseri countered that focusing on a single feature overlooks Meta’s broader efforts to safeguard minors. Meta Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg is expected to testify later in the trial as the company defends itself against allegations that its social media platforms are knowingly addictive. “There’s no denying that these platforms are addictive, talk to any who says they’re begging themselves to be able to stop doomscrolling and you know that they’re addictive,” Benavidez said. Mosseri is expected to return to the stand to continue his testimony.

headlines.title: Dolly Parton remembered in Bay Area for music, advocacy and literacy impact
headlines.description: Dolly Parton’s legacy extends far beyond her decades of music, leaving a lasting impression in the Bay Area through both her artistic influence and her philanthropic work. In the children’s section of the main San Francisco Public Library, a life-sized cutout of the country music icon highlights her Imagination Library project. Over the past year, her partnership with the library system has delivered approximately 60,000 books nationwide to children enrolled in the program. “And even if they didn’t know her personally, she will have had a role in their life,” said Theresa Zighera, deputy director of the San Francisco Department of Early Childhood. “A really clear and meaningful role.” The effort ensures a lasting legacy even for youth unfamiliar with her extensive music catalog. “She’s left an impression on generations of people through her music, movies and television,” NBC Bay Area reporter Sergio Quintana said. “And even now Dolly Parton’s legacy will include leaving an impression on children, through books.” The San Francisco Public Library is one of more than 2,700 program partners across the country. Each local partner covers half the cost of mailing books directly to children, while the Dolly Parton Foundation or state grants fund the remaining half. “I know for Dolly, it was spurred by her own father who had struggles reading,” said Ruben Balderas, an early learning coordinator. “And she wanted to give kids, really, a leg up.” Music remained her primary gift to the world. During Pride Month, the San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus paid tribute to Parton with a performance of her classic hit “9 to 5.” “I think the LGBTQ+ community connects with her so much because she woke up every day, decided how she wanted to live and did so courageously and publicly,” said Jacob Stensberg, artistic director of the San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus. “And in doing so made us all believe that we could do that too.” Throughout her career, Parton performed numerous times across the Bay Area, including a 2005 appearance at the Hardly Strictly Bluegrass festival. She also appeared in local media interviews, including a December 2022 segment with NBC Bay Area’s Marcus Washington, where Washington asked if they could sing “We Wish You a Merry Christmas” together. “Aha, I don’t know if I know it well enough, are you going to take lead?” Parton joked in response. Following the announcement of her passing, her nephew Bryan Seaver shared a final message with her fans. “May God Bless Dolly Parton. And may God bless you all,” Seaver said. “She will always love you.”

headlines.title: San Jose police officer injured, suspect killed following shootout
headlines.description: A San Jose police officer was in critical but stable condition late Tuesday at Santa Clara Valley Medical Center after being shot by an armed robbery suspect earlier in the afternoon, according to police. The shooting occurred in the area of Lick Avenue and Goodyear Street. An advisor to San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan said the mayor planned to visit the officer at the hospital, and his office later indicated that the visit took place. A possible second person involved in the shooting was taken to the hospital, though their condition remains unknown. A heavy police presence was reported nearby at Almaden Avenue and Floyd Street, where a local resident reported seeing officers from the San Jose Police Department and deputies from the Santa Clara County Sheriff’s Office with guns drawn, alongside a potential response from university police. Witnesses reported seeing an individual down on the ground and expressed concern that a subject may have barricaded themselves, though police have not verified those accounts. A local family in the area told NBC Bay Area that a suspect entered their home and held family members hostage before escaping. Authorities have not confirmed that account or stated whether that incident is connected to the shooting. By late Tuesday evening, much of the scene outside Santa Clara Valley Medical Center — where caution tape previously blocked the entrance alongside a heavy law enforcement presence — had dispersed and quieted down. Department public information officers noted that the investigation remains active and ongoing, with additional official details regarding what led up to the gunfire to be released as they become available.
headlines.source: Pete Suratos, Ali Reid and Erik Gabaldon

headlines.title: Results revealed from San Jose poll to rename downtown plaza
headlines.description: Results from a public poll to rename San Jose’s downtown plaza were revealed Tuesday. San Jose is looking to rename the plaza, which for 33 years carried the name of late labor leader Cesar Chavez, after his name was removed in March following allegations of sexual assault and misconduct. The top two choices from the poll are Plaza de San Jose, which led with 40% of the vote, and Farmworkers Plaza. About 10,000 San Jose residents participated in the multiple-choice poll to rename the plaza. A committee with San Jose Parks, Recreation and Neighborhood Services will now recommend the top choice to the parks and recreation commission, who will then vote on Sept. 2 whether to advance it to the city council for consideration. San Jose’s city council is expected to make a final decision on the plaza’s new name in late October. San Jose Mar 24 San Jose Mar 19 San Jose Mar 16, 2024 San Jose leaders unveil beautification of Plaza de Cesar Chavez
